_exec_summary.SummaryText:
Chevron Phillips Chemical Company LP is an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of Chevron Phillips Chemical Company LLC, one of the world's top producers of olefins and polyolefins and a leading supplier of aromatics, alpha olefins, styrenics, specialty chemicals, plastic piping and polymer resins. With approximately 5,000 employees, the LLC and its affiliates own more than $10.5 billion in assets, including 37 manufacturing and research facilities in eight countries. Chevron Phillips Chemical Company LLC is equally owned by Chevron U.S.A. Inc., an indirect wholly-owned subsidiary of Chevron Corporation, and by wholly-owned subsidiaries of Phillips 66, and is headquartered in The Woodlands, Texas.

The Chevron Phillips Chemical Company LP Orange Plant is located in Orange, Texas and operates two reactors that produce high density polyethylene (HDPE). The HDPE manufacturing process uses various regulated flammable chemicals such as ethylene, isobutane, propane, hydrogen, and isopentane to produce HDPE. This facility includes two (2) Risk Management Plan (RMP) covered processes, that have been identified as the CPF, ERU, & H-Line HDPE Polyethylene and GPO & G-line Polyethylene. The two (2) processes contain mixtures of flammable regulated substances in greater than threshold quantities and are classified as Prevention Program 3 facilities.

The following is a summary of the general accident prevention programs in place at the Chevron Phillips Chemical Company LP, Orange Plant. The Orange Plant is an OSHA (Occupational Safety and Health Administration) Process Safety Management (PSM) regulated facility. The elements of the Orange Plant's PSM program / OSHA PSM standard has been in place since 1992, which essentially mirror the prevention program requirement of the Environmental Protection Agency's (EPA) RMP standard.

Employee Participation

The intent of employee participation is to ensure that Orange Plant employees are informed, consulted and involved in all aspects of

process safety management. Examples of employee participation range from reviewing Process Safety Information (PSI) and Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs) to serving on Process Hazard Analysis (PHA) teams. The Orange Plant also uses other processes such as company communication tools, Reinforcement Based Safety (RBS), and OSHA's Voluntary Protection Program (VPP) to keep employees engaged and provide periodic reminders to the employees that their process safety concerns and suggestions are welcome.

Process Safety Information (PSI)

The Orange plant compiles and maintains written process safety information to enable both the employer and employee to effectively identify and understand the hazards posed by the process. Written PSI provides employees with baseline information to identify hazards of the chemicals used or produced in the process, information about the technology of the process, and information about the equipment in the process. This PSI provides the foundation for performing the unit Process Hazards Analyses, developing operating procedures, and determining the applicability of Management of Change (MOC).

Process Hazard Analysis (PHA)

A Process Hazard Analysis is a systematic evaluation of all aspects of the process (equipment, chemicals, technology, and procedures) to identify the potential hazards associated with the processing and handling of highly hazardous chemicals. PHAs are performed on existing and new units in all of the Orange Plant's processes. The Checklist and Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP), or other appropriate equivalent methodologies, were used to perform the PHAs on each covered process at the Orange plant. A PHA results in action items (findings/recommendations) that identify and address perceived potential hazards. The action items are prioritized for management and employee resolution using the scheme below: The Orange Plant uses Layers of Protection Analysis methodology (commonly referred to as LOPA) to integrate proces

s risk management into a unified, comprehensive program. Independent Protection Layers (IPLs) are systems used to mitigate serious environmental and process safety risk, identified during the PHA. IPLs include specific and identified standard operating procedures, alarms with operator response, safety instrumented systems, emergency shutdown systems, and protective devices. IPLs can be viewed as one of the first lines of defense against a potential incident by decreasing the likelihood of a potential incident. IPL analysis provides the risk assessment methodology for the PHA which is an integral part of the PSM program. If an action item arises from the analysis it will be managed and tracked to completion.

Operating Procedures

Written standard operating procedures (SOP) provide clear instructions for the safe operation and control of a process and associated equipment. SOPs are readily accessible to operations personnel in the control room and all other employees via an electronic delivery system. The SOPs address various phases of operation, such as initial startup, normal operations, temporary operations, emergency operations, emergency shutdown, normal shutdown, and subsequent startup. SOPs also address safety and health considerations and information on Safe Work Practices. Revisions to SOPs may be prompted as a result of MOC, PHA, an annual review of SOPs or input from employees who may use the SOPs.

Training

The Orange Plant has implemented a comprehensive training program for its employees, especially those involved in operating a process. Operator training has been developed to equip operators with the knowledge and skill necessary to safely and proficiently perform their job duties. This training emphasizes specific safety and health hazards, emergency operations including shutdown, and safe work practices applicable to the employee's job tasks. Written tests, observation, demonstration, and peer evaluations are used to verify the training. Refresher t

raining/certification is provided every three years to operations personnel. Training in safe work practices is provided to employees during new employee safety orientation, annual safety training, special classes, computer based training, and electronic notices of change.

Contractors

Contract employees at the Orange Plant provide labor for general maintenance or repairs, turnarounds, major renovations, construction, demolition, equipment installation or specialty work on or adjacent to covered processes. Thus, their actions may have an influence on process safety. The Orange Plant informs contractors of known potential fire, explosion or toxic release hazards related to the contractor's work and the process as well as the emergency action plan, safe work practices and sign-in/sign-out requirements for the Orange Plant. The contract employer is responsible for assuring that each contract employee is trained in the work practices necessary to safely perform his/her job.

Mechanical Integrity

The intent of the mechanical integrity program is to provide a management system that ensures: (1) the equipment is maintained in a manner to prevent or minimize the consequences of a catastrophic release of a highly hazardous chemical and (2) the equipment is maintained by trained and qualified personnel to ensure its continued integrity. Mechanical integrity covered equipment at the Orange Plant includes the following types of equipment: pressure vessels, storage tanks, piping, valves, relief and vent systems, emergency shutdown systems, controls, and pumps. The basic aspects of the mechanical integrity system include: (1) design and construction requirements; (2) preventive maintenance practices; (3) testing and inspection; (4) repair, modification and alteration procedures; and (5) inspector and craftsman training and qualifications.

Safe Work Practices

The Orange Plant has many safe work practices that promote worker and process safety. Examples of these include (1) hot

work permits to control work involving flame or spark-producing operations; (2) confined space entry permits to ensure adequate safety precautions have been taken prior to entering vessels, tanks and other confined spaces; (3) lockout/tagout procedures to guarantee isolation of energy sources prior to working on equipment; and (4) pressure-relief device (PRD) removal procedures to ensure adequate alternate relief paths are available prior to removal of any PRD and (5) interlock and alarm bypassing procedures to ensure that critical process controls are managed properly. These procedures, along with others, form a system to help make certain that operations and maintenance activities are performed in a safe manner.

Management of Change and Pre-Startup Safety Review

The Orange Plant has a comprehensive system to manage changes to processes. Changes may introduce new hazards or compromise safeguards incorporated into the original design of the process and must be reviewed prior to their implementation. This system requires that changes to items such as process equipment, chemicals, technology (including process-operating conditions), software, procedures (including operating, maintenance, and safe work) and emergency procedures be properly reviewed for potential hazards and authorized before being implemented. This system requires that any change executed address the following: the technical basis for the proposed change; the impact of the change on safety and health; modifications to operating procedures; necessary time period for change; and authorization requirements for the proposed change. Affected process safety information (e.g., mechanical, electrical/instrument, chemical, and operating limits) and procedures (e.g., operating, maintenance, and safe work) are updated to incorporate these changes. In addition, operating and maintenance personnel are provided necessary training on the change. The Orange Plant conducts a Pre-startup Safety Review (PSSR) for any

new facility or facility modification that requires a change in the process safety information. A PSSR is conducted for the following types of changes: equipment, facilities, and/or process chemicals, technology, and software. The PSSR serves as a final verification prior to the introduction of highly hazardous chemicals into the process at a new facility and conducted prior to start-up, commissioning, or engagement of the change, for existing, modified facilities. The PSSR must confirm the following: a PHA has been performed for new facilities and that PHA recommendations have been resolved; MOC requirements have been executed for changes to modified facilities; construction and equipment installation is in accordance with design specifications; training of each employee involved in operating a process has been completed; and, safety, operating, maintenance, and emergency procedures are in place and are adequate.

Incident Investigation

Incidents, which resulted in or reasonably could have resulted in a catastrophic release of a highly hazardous chemical, are investigated by a cross-section of plant personnel. The composition of investigation teams varies with the complexity of the incident, but the underlying philosophy is one of employee/contractor involvement, as appropriate. Once the results of the incident investigation are available, incidents including findings and recommended actions are summarized and communicated throughout the facility. The full incident investigation report is available to any employee/contractor.

Compliance Audits

The Orange Plant conducts compliance audits to periodically evaluate the effectiveness of the PSM Program; to ensure that each program element complies with the standard; and to ascertain whether the elements from internal procedures and practices are adequate and are being implemented. Compliance audits are conducted at least every three years. The audit team is comprised of a variety of disciplines who use a set of self-

audit checklists based on the OSHA PSM and EPA RMP standards. Audit findings and responses are entered and maintained in a computer-based tracking system. The final resolution of each finding is documented, and the two most recent audit reports are retained.

The Orange Plant operates an extensive emergency response program to protect worker and public safety as well as the environment. The Orange Plant has several written documents, which detail the actions to be taken in response to an unwanted release of a highly hazardous chemical. General Plant Safety Rules provide basic instructions to employees for reporting and responding to an emergency. The Orange Plant Emergency Action Plan further provides detailed instructions and information used by essential personnel with regard to the emergency planning and response systems that are implemented at the Orange Plant.

The Emergency Action Plan is developed and updated by a cross-section of plant personnel under the direction of the Safety Department. A significant part of the Emergency Action Plan is the Orange Plant Emergency Response Team. This team provides a significant part of all emergency response services for the facility. This team is comprised of employees who voluntarily participate as members of the team. Membership requires participation in a rigorous training and qualification program. Once qualified, each team member is expected to respond to emergency alarms while at work or if called out after their normal work shift.
The program consists of procedures for responding to various emergencies, including a small incidental emergency, plant-wide emergency, an external emergency, a hurricane or severe weather emergency, and a bomb threat. The Incident Command System is used to manage all emergency response situations. The Orange Plant Emergency Response Team, a volunteer group of trained employees, responds to all plant emergencies to help minimize loss of life, property and to provide emergency medical car

e to the injured. Trained Emergency Responders are onsite 24 hours per day.

The Orange Plant is a member of the Orange County Local Emergency Planning Committee, Sabine Neches Chiefs, and Southeast Texas Alerting Network.

The CPChem Orange Plant had no RMP reportable incident in the five years prior to the submittal of this RMP.

Various safety measures are in place to prevent the release of flammable chemicals. Some examples of these measures include: (pressure relief valves, hydrocarbon area detectors, remote valves to isolate the process, administrative controls, operating procedures, Safety Instrumented Systems, etc,).

This facility is covered by OSHA PSM regulations and numerous EPA and Texas Commission on Environmental Quality regulatory requirements designed to limit the impact on the environment and to the best of our knowledge we are in substantial compliance with these regulations.

Continuous improvement in safety and environmental performance will be achieved through several practices including employee safety processes, Tenets of Operation guiding principles, Operational Excellence System, and other employee involvement programs. Planned changes to improve safety at the Orange Plant are reviewed and adjusted annually. Improvements are also included in the yearly budgets and incorporated into the performance management systems / practices throughout the organization. These planned changes include, but are not limited to safety related capital projects, safety programs / initiatives, procedure improvements, and SOP validations
